# Cancer of unknown primary

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Hematology and oncology > Other hemato-oncologic conditions > Cancer of unknown primary*

[Original Article Link](/library/eI0xbh)

---

## Summary

Cancer of unknown primary (CUP) is a <u>metastatic</u> cancer that has no identified site of origin following the completion of a standard oncologic evaluation. CUPs are a heterogeneous group of cancers with different histopathologies and varied manifestations. Collectively, CUPs account for approximately 3–5% of all malignancies. The initial diagnostic workup of CUP is focused on trying to locate the site of the primary <u>tumor</u> based on the imaging and <u>histopathology</u> findings. If a primary site cannot be identified, the cancer is classified into a favorable or unfavorable subgroup. CUPs in the favorable subgroup have clinical manifestations, <u>histopathology</u> findings, or biomarkers similar to known primary cancers and are treated with standard <u>anticancer treatment</u> regimens for the equivalent primary cancer. Patients with a <u>tumor</u> in the unfavorable subgroup (80–85%) receive empiric low-dose <u>chemotherapy</u>, but the median survival is poor (typically less than one year).

---

## Diagnosis

### Approach




* Work up for the most likely primary cancer based on symptoms.

* If symptoms are nonspecific, consider <u>common origins of cancer metastases</u>.

* In palpable <u>lymphadenopathy</u>, consider patterns of <u>lymphatic drainage</u> to determine a likely primary cancer.

* No primary site identified: Perform routine studies for CUP.

* Primary site remains unknown: Perform additional studies based on presentation and <u>histopathology</u>.

Palpable lymph nodes




### Routine studies for CUP [[3]](/library/Dlc1_c0)[[6]](/library/P-cWxU0)[[7]](/library/jS1_zT0)




#### <u>Laboratory studies</u>




* Assessment for organ/marrow involvement: <u>CBC</u>, <u>CMP</u>, <u>liver chemistries</u>

* Prognostication: <u>LDH</u>  [[3]](/library/Dlc1_c0)





#### Imaging




* All patients: CT thorax, abdomen, and <u>pelvis</u> with IV contrast

* Women and <u>transmen</u>: <u>mammography</u>





#### Analysis of the <u>tumor</u>  [[3]](/library/Dlc1_c0)[[8]](/library/eScxAb0)




* <u>Histopathology</u>

* Well-differentiated or moderately well-differentiated <u>adenocarcinomas</u> (∼ 60%)

* Poorly differentiated <u>carcinoma</u> (25–30%)

* <u>Squamous cell carcinoma</u> (5%)

* Undifferentiated <u>neoplasm</u> (5%)

* Neuroendocrine (1%)

* <u>Immunohistochemistry</u>: e.g., <u>cytokeratin</u>, <u>vimentin</u> (see “<u>Immunohistochemical markers</u>”)

* <u>Gene expression</u> assay

* Molecular profiling





> [!WARNING]
> Patients who have had a <u>mastectomy</u> should have an <u>MRI</u> to assess residual <u>breast</u> tissue.




### Additional studies [[3]](/library/Dlc1_c0)[[6]](/library/P-cWxU0)[[7]](/library/jS1_zT0)




* Women and <u>transmen</u> with axillary <u>adenocarcinoma</u>: <u>MRI</u> <u>breast</u>

* Midline <u>neoplastic</u> disease: <u>alpha-fetoprotein</u>, <u>hCG</u>

* Men and <u>transwomen</u> with <u>adenocarcinoma</u> <u>metastatic</u> to bone: <u>prostate-specific antigen</u> (<u>PSA</u>)

* <u>Neuroendocrine tumor</u>: <u>octreotide</u> scan, <u>chromogranin A</u>

* Cervical <u>lymph node</u> <u>squamous cell carcinoma</u>: <u>laryngoscopy</u> and <u>PET-CT scan</u>  [[9]](/library/cS1aAT0)

* Abdominal symptoms: <u>colonoscopy</u> and <u>gastroscopy</u>

* Hilar or <u>mediastinal lymph node</u> involvement: <u>bronchoscopy</u>





> [!TIP]
> <u>Peripheral blood tumor markers</u> should not be performed routinely because they are frequently not specific for <u>tumor</u> sites. They may, however, be helpful in certain clinical presentations. [[5]](/library/PS1W-T0)




> [!TIP]
> <u>PET-CT scan</u> may be useful in patients with CUP who have cervical <u>adenopathy</u> or a single <u>metastatic</u> <u>tumor</u> site; it has limited utility in other patients. [[3]](/library/Dlc1_c0)
